Buzite
BUZ-ite
n. (the designation of Elihu, the fourth speaker in Job; named twice)
A gentilic from Buz, Hebrew Buzi; Buz was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and the name also belongs to a people of the east; used twice, Job 32:2 and 32:6.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

Buzite is the designation of Elihu, who had sat silent through the long dispute and then spoke: “Then was kindled the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram: against Job was his wrath kindled, because he justified himself rather than God” (Job 32:2). He gives his own reason for waiting: “And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said, I am young, and ye are very old; wherefore I was afraid, and durst not shew you mine opinion” (Job 32:6). His argument turns on a principle he states at once, that age is not the source of understanding: “But there is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding” (Job 32:8). Elihu is the one speaker in the book whom God does not rebuke. The three friends are named and censured by the LORD Himself at the end: “And it was so, that after the LORD had spoken these words unto Job, the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath” (Job 42:7). Elihu is not in that sentence, and his speeches turn the book from the friends' accusations toward the greatness of God, which is the subject of the whirlwind.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Buzite, a descendant of Buz, or a native of the region of that name; the designation of Elihu in Job.

Buzite is a gentilic from Buz, Hebrew Buzi.

Buz was a son of Nahor, the brother of Abraham.

It occurs twice in the Authorized Version, Job 32:2 and 32:6.

It designates Elihu the son of Barachel, of the kindred of Ram.

Elihu is the fourth and last of the human speakers in Job.

Key Scripture

Job 32:2 — "Then was kindled the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram: against Job was his wrath kindled, because he justified himself rather than God."

Job 32:6 — "And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said, I am young, and ye are very old; wherefore I was afraid, and durst not shew you mine opinion."

Job 32:8 — "But there is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding."

Job 42:7 — "And it was so, that after the LORD had spoken these words unto Job, the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath."

Modern Corruption

The Elihu speeches are called a later insertion, and his argument lumped in with the friends', where the LORD's own rebuke at the end names the three and passes him by.

expand to see more

Critical treatments of Job commonly excise chapters 32 to 37 as a later addition, on the ground that Elihu appears without introduction and is never answered. The book is composed to make that reading unlikely. Elihu's silence is explained in the text by his youth; his entrance prepares the whirlwind by turning the subject from Job's case to God's greatness and God's teaching through affliction; and when the LORD apportions blame He names Eliphaz and “thy two friends” (Job 42:7) and says nothing against Elihu. An interpolation would be the easiest thing to condemn, and the text does not condemn it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Elihu states: understanding is not a function of years but a gift, for “there is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding” (Job 32:8). A young man waited his turn, honoured his elders, and then said what none of them had said.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Gentilic from Buz; Elihu the Buzite, Job 32:2.
